speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition; Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: FEDERAL PARTICIPATION IN PROPOSED PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a question to the right hon. Prime Minister. Will the Prime Minister pay heed to the strong demand from across Canada for federal government leadership and personally attend the confederation of tomorrow conference as a means of showing some interest in a matter which is of concern to all Canadians?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: FEDERAL PARTICIPATION IN PROPOSED PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Order, please. I wish to bring to the attention of the Leader of the Opposition that the question is obviously couched in the form of an argument. That is not in accordance with the rules. The question should be asked directly.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition; Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: FEDERAL PARTICIPATION IN PROPOSED PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: I shall rephrase the question, Mr. Speaker. Will the Prime Minister personally attend the confederation of tomorrow conference that is being held and which is of such great interest to all Canadians?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: FEDERAL PARTICIPATION IN PROPOSED PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker. This, of course, is an interprovincial conference. I do not know of any such conference which has been attended by the prime minister of this country, important though such a conference undoubtedly is. It has been made quite clear by the premier of Ontario that this is an interprovincial conference at which matters of provincial co-operation will be discussed by the governments of the provinces. Perhaps as a result of that discussion the provinces, or some of them, will be able to put on the agenda of the federal-provincial conference in January some subjects that can be discussed there on a federal-provincial basis.
Meanwhile the government will be represented by observers as is customary at provincial conferences. The four federal observers will be Mr. Jean Beetz, assistant secretary of the cabinet; Mr. Carl Goldenberg, special
adviser to the Minister of Justice on constitutional matters; Mr. A. W. Johnson, assistant deputy minister of finance; and Mr. Marc Lalonde, special adviser to the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition; Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: FEDERAL PARTICIPATION IN PROPOSED PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Does the Prime Minister not think Canada's confederation is far too important to be left to officials, and that the sooner he stops making speeches and starts attending these conferences the better it will be for Canada?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: FEDERAL PARTICIPATION IN PROPOSED PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Order, please.

subtopic: FEDERAL PARTICIPATION IN PROPOSED PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: No one is more concerned with the confederation of Canada than I am.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: FEDERAL PARTICIPATION IN PROPOSED PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Order, please. I wonder if the Leader of the Opposition does not think his question is more an argument than a question formulated according to the custom of the house.

speechtext: Order. House again in committee of supply, estimates of the Treasury Board for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1968. Vote No. 1. This vote will be found on page 560 of the blue book. The details are found on page 561.
1. Departmental administration, including grants as detailed in the estimates, $4,478,700.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall vote No. 1 carry?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. J. Benson (Minister of National Revenue and President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend at this time to make a general statement with respect to Treasury Board activities. I made a rather long statement during the budget debate concerning activities in the area of government administration carried out by the Treasury Board. Due to the limited time available for consideration of estimates I believe it would now be better if I allowed hon. members opposite and on this side to raise any questions they may have with respect to the Treasury Board estimates, and then I will do my utmost to answer them.
However, I would like to pay tribute to Dr. Davidson, secretary of the Treasury Board, who has done a tremendous job in reorganizing the Treasury Board and in obtaining assistant deputy ministers in the persons of Mr. Cloutier, formerly of the civil service commission, Mr. Doug Love and Mr. Don Yoemans, who are looking after the three divisions of the Treasury Board, the personnel, management organization and program branches. I think they are doing a very good job putting into effect the advances in administrative techniques which were suggested first of all in the Glassco commission report and which have been carried further by the introduction of computer equipment in many departments, and by the introduction of finance officers and a new system of financial management in various departments of government.
I would be more than pleased to deal with any questions hon. members may wish to raise with respect to these estimates.

Mr. Chairman, the core of fiscal management and responsibility in government is Treasury Board. This is the afternoon of Hallowe'en, and perhaps it is as good a day as any to discuss our existing

financial status. It needs no spooks or banshees, no seers, to determine that something is radically wrong at the core.
Hear, hear.

Let me put it this way, sir. Government competence or incompetence can be most directly and immediately determined by the activities of that compact group of cabinet ministers who constitute Treasury Board. There, within that small, exclusive body lies the test of fiscal responsibility, of administrative efficiency, of the utility and practicality of most government plans and operations. As well, Treasury Board decisions affect directly all aspects of the national economy in both the public and private sectors.
With no wish to be severe on the genial President of the Treasury Board I submit that Treasury Board has been weighed and found desperately wanting. Its failures, which I intend to describe this afternoon, deserve the outright censure of this committee and in the proper time, the sooner the better, will be repudiated by the country.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
There is a variety of reasons; the variety is equalled only by their abundance. I am disappointed by the absence this afternoon of any useful or meaningful statement from the President of the Treasury Board in introducing these estimates. This is the clearest indication of the growing arrogance of the government and its lack of concern for financial responsibility. There is one thing about which I can agree with the minister, and that is his tribute to the secretary of the Treasury Board. Dr. George Davidson is a man in whom I have unbounded confidence. I only wish the ministers who sit on the Treasury Board had the wisdom to follow his judgment and advice.
Last Thursday the Leader of the Opposition, in rather vivid and eloquent terms, exposed the fiscal incompetence of this government. The fact is that mistaken fiscal policies centring on the total failure to establish priorities in expenditures, resulting in an almost complete lack of genuine fiscal or monetary control, are gravely endangering the future of the nation and if persisted in could bring about a disastrous financial crisis. I do not use these words lightly, sir. For these factors the President of the Treasury Board and the Treasury Board itself must share the responsibility equally with the Minister of Finance. It is the function of the
October 31, 1967

Treasury Board to establish priorities, to weigh one requirement against another, to exercise a strong and firm rein upon runaway spenders. My plea this afternoon to the President of the Treasury Board is to change course at once, to set up genuine priorities and stick to them, and to restore adequate control over governmental expenditure. I ask him to do so before it is too late.
I do not wish to sound in any way an alarmist, for I have unlimited confidence in Canada. But informed economic observers are genuinely alarmed, and with good reason. It is not just a case of spend, spend, spend; it goes much beyond that. They neglect even to try to control inflationary pressures; we have actual encouragement of the establishment of the highest interest rates in history, rates which have become unconscionable usury; disregard of what Fraser Robertson describes as "an incipient old fashioned money panic"; failure even to attempt to restore confidence and faith in the investment market. These are all symptoms of the extent to which the President of the Treasury Board and the Minister of Finance, as well as the Treasury Board itself, have avoided responsibility and positive action. I suggest they prove that the government is bankrupt equally of ideas and responsibility. The respected London Economist speaks of the massive indifference to the symptoms. My submission is that we cannot afford longer to mask our eyes to the realities of the incipient crisis which this government has brought upon the nation.
The estimates which this Treasury Board has submitted to this committee for this fiscal year, with supplementaries, amount to $9,646 million, to which must be added $645 million in loans and advances for a total of almost $10,300 million. Additional supplementaries for the year will no doubt boost this figure to approximately $10,600 million. This is the amount which must be raised from the taxpayers and from the market.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member would permit a question. He tied in loans and advances. Of course he realizes the latter do not have to be raised from Canadian taxpayers.

I did not catch exactly what the minister said, but I think he will find that I said this amount will have to be raised from the Canadian taxpayers or the market. The minister knows perfectly well that he is having even greater difficulty in raising it from the market than in raising it from the taxpayers.
Supply-Treasury Board
The last full year of the previous government showed total expenditures of $6,364 million, broken down between $6,230 million in expenditures and $134 million in loans and advances. In other words the demands of this government upon the taxpayers and the market over a period of approximately 4J years have grown and increased by almost four and a quarter billion, or at a rate of almost a billion dollars per year. If this government were to remain in office for two more years, a fate from which Canada should certainly be protected, and the rate of growth of government expenditures should persist, this government will have doubled the level of spending in just six years.
Someone in the government is feeding out leaks about allegedly massive cuts to be made by the Treasury Board in next year's estimates of up to three quarters of a billion dollars. Indeed, I read this morning that cuts of $825 million were to be made. What is not said is that these are supposedly cuts from the estimates as submitted by each department for next year, and not cutbacks from this year's estimates. This three quarters of a billion is just a phony, unrealistic figure plucked from the air. My experience as a member of Treasury Board and earlier as parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance indicates that it is very rare that Treasury Board cuts amount to less than 10 per cent of the estimates of the various departments as first submitted. So the alleged three quarters of a billion dollars is not any more and is perhaps less than would be normal in any year as a cutback from the original submission of estimates.
The latest leaked gossip is that $175 million or $200 million is to be cut off the estimates now before the committee of supply. Yet the Minister of Finance and the President of the Treasury Board have declined to answer the questions of the hon, member for Perth and others or to say whether these cuts will be made and, if so, where. This, despite the fact that the guillotine will fall on Thursday night and parliament will be deprived of any further right of discussion. In any event, a cut of even $200 million would be less than 2 per cent of these estimates. What a fabulous success that would be-2 per cent.
What I am pleading for this afternoon to the President of the Treasury Board and his colleagues on that board is the establishment of a genuine system of priorities. I am not asking for a cut in all expenditures right.
October 31, 1967

Supply-Treasury Board across the board. Indeed, there are some expenditures I should like to see increased, and I will mention one before I conclude this afternoon. There is nothing inconsistent in that approach. What I want the President of the Treasury Board to do is to establish priorities and take this house as well as the public into his confidence by telling us what priorities have been established, and the target dates. I suggest that only such action can bring about a restoration of confidence, an easing of the financial uneasiness existing among economists and on all the markets, a halt to inflationary pressures and bring about a rationalization of the interest structure.
The government has its choice; establish priorities and do so now or face fiscal and economic disaster. I use strong words because the times require plain speaking. This is the time to say no to the big spenders. I venture to submit that one of the biggest problems is that the Prime Minister is almost congenitally incapable of saying no. Indeed, if he had been born of the other sex it would have been quite disastrous.
I wish to deal briefly with the government's attitude toward parliamentary control of the estimates and of expenditures. The very bedrock of our parliamentary institution is the absolute control by this chamber of the public purse. The misuse last autumn of the contingency vote and the abuse by transfers from other votes drove a horse and cart through every known principle of responsible parliamentary government. I suggest it was of the most dubious legal validity, but irrespective of that it was constitutionally unacceptable. It was "an erosion of parliament's traditional role in controlling public funds", to quote the words of the Auditor General of Canada.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Professor Norman Ward, on page 1 of his book "The Public Purse", states the theory and practice of parliamentary control of finance to be as follows:
Underlying all the others are two principles, both of which have to be supported by a number [DOT]of subsidiary principles and practices:
(1)	The executive should have no income which is not granted to it, or otherwise sanctioned by parliament.
(2)	The executive should make no expenditures except those approved by parliament in ways approved by parliament.
W. Ivor Jennings, in his great work on parliament, indicates that the principle of

control of expenditures on behalf of the public is to be found in Magna Carta and therefore existed even before a parliament in modern form was known. R. McGregor Dawson, at page 229 of his book, "The Government of Canada", speaks of these principles and adds:
-collectively they place the cabinet in a position where its responsibility in all financial matters is complete and ineluctable.
Sir, the contingency item, which until this last year was under the Department of Finance, was intended to be nothing more nor less than the petty cash account of the government to provide for minor unforeseen expenditures of the government. For quite a number of years the amount was $1| million and the language of the item was very strictly confined. When this government came to office the amount was $3 million. In these estimates the President of the Treasury Board asks that we vote $45 million for petty cash, $45 million for unforeseen contingencies. Poor old Mr. C. D. Howe got into such great difficulty when he said, "what's a million."
Judged by the government's other irresponsibilities perhaps this can be understood, but I suggest it is something to augment an item in the estimates 15 times over in just four years and to change its language and purpose. The change in the language of the item is too clever by half; it is an attempt to deceive parliament. Some of my colleagues will deal with this later in the debate. What I say now is that a petty cash account of $45 million is intolerable. An item worded in the form to which the present item has been changed is a denial of the basis of House of Commons control of the executive. Imagine the arrogance of a government which admits its incompetence in estimating to such an extent that it needs a $45 million contingency fund for minor unforeseen items!
I agree most wholeheartedly that provision should be made for the payment of public service salaries in days of parliamentary warfare, and I introduced a private member's bill last autumn which would so provide. I believe the pay lists should be separated from the other items. Civil servants and their livelihood should never be made the pawn of political infighting and should not suffer from parliamentary brinkmanship. I assert with the greatest confidence, however, that this Commons chamber must now reassert its basic purpose, its right to deny supply and to bring a government to its knees. If we vote a
October 31, 1967

petty cash item of $45 million and if transfers within items are unlimited by the Financial Administration Act, as this government arrogantly asserts, then the Commons has lost its most fundamental purpose. The executive will have made themselves the masters not only of parliament but of the people.
Earlier I mentioned that the establishment of a genuine system of priorities in governmental programming might in some cases require increased spending. I should like to discuss briefly one subject in respect of which I have some difficulty in using measured and moderate language in view of the government's dilatoriness and neglect.
Members of this house have been urging year after year and month after month an adjustment in pensions for retired public servants, including the members of the armed forces and the R.C.M.P. Finally, a reluctant President of the Treasury Board and the government yielded to the request and agreed to a reference to the special joint committee on the public service. Last May 8 that committee reported unanimously in favour of such increases. It was a knowledgeable and responsible committee of senators and members. But what has happened to the report? Apparently it has been pigeonholed in the deepest recesses of the east block. A score of times there have been questions on the orders of the day addressed to the Prime Minister, to the Minister of Finance and to the President of the Treasury Board; twice there have been adjournment debates. All this has resulted in the same inconclusive result-"under cabinet consideration", "decision in due course."
"Due course" is so long overdue that it is clear the government is off course. It is an open secret that the President of the Treasury Board would like to adopt the committee's report to which his parliamentary secretary was a party. I thought that when the former minister of transport fixed up his own increased pension by becoming president of the Canadian Transport Commission we had lost the chief enemy in the cabinet of effective action. But no. Somewhere, somehow, there remain in the cabinet men or a woman who oppose justice for our retired public servants. What about the Minister of Public Works, a man who represents so many public servants? I reiterate what I have said previously. He has a special obligation in this matter and he should either persuade his colleagues in the cabinet to accept the just demands of his constituents or he should
Supply-Treasury Board resign in protest. I suggest that the time for action is long past. Other countries have acted long ago. Other countries, and indeed our own provinces, have instituted a variety of systems of pension adjustment.
Time after time-and I shall not do it again this afternoon-I have placed on the record details of the increases achieved in other countries which face the same problems and are confronted with the same issues with which we are confronted. In Britain a formula increase is and has been for many years an accepted legislative fact; equally is such the case in the United States, in France, in Italy, in Australia and in New Zealand. What these countries have done can be done here in Canada without violation of any principle. I submit that it is a special obligation of the government to be an exemplary employer and to set the example for private industry.
It has been the action, or lack of action, on the part of this government which I described earlier that has promoted the unprecedented skyrocketing of the cost of living and has resulted in the eroding of pensions which frugal persons thought wholly adequate for their retirement. Pensions paid for in hard dollars have been eroded by creeping inflation which has accelerated to runaway inflation. The dollars drawn in the form of superannuation in many, many cases are worth less than 50 per cent of the dollars which were used to buy the pension entitlement. Elderly men and women who gave their best in other days watch hopelessly while their lifetime contributions to superannuation dwindle into insignificance. I submit that precedents for action across the world are manifold and that only the Canadian government refuses to act. e (3:40 p.m.)
I plead this afternoon with the President of the Treasury Board to end this day this charade of inaction and to bring hope and renewed belief in Canada to the thousands of former public servants who have served her so well.
One of the results of the legislation at the last session regarding the public service has been to transfer classification in the public service to the Treasury Board. I have grave reservations about this. I do not separate so casually the alleged managerial function of classification and the allegedly totally independent function of recruitment and appointment. Perhaps that is because I do not bow down to and worship all of the Glassco report.
3684
October 31, 1967

Supply-Treasury Board
The classification review of the public service has been a morale destroyer and a source of major personal tragedies from its inception, and it does not improve. "Red circling" is a familiar term. It bears no sinister connotation to those who have not experienced it. What I am unable to understand is how the very best personnel officials in our country have been guilty of some of the greatest public relations gaucheries respecting their own fellow employees.
We were told at the outset that a complete classification review was a prerequisite to the institution of collective bargaining in the public service-indeed, a sine qua non. Now there has been a total reversal of this argument. According to the return tabled on September 25, 1967 to my question No. 335, the completion of the classification review will depend upon the progress of collective bargaining negotiations. Such a chicken and egg argument I have seldom heard. While this goes on there have been many public servants who have been shifted into blind alleys and allowed to languish in the still waters of official neglect. I suggest to the President of the Treasury Board that the clean-up of the "red circle" program is long overdue. Through the loss in morale Canada has lost much more than if the classification review had never been undertaken. I suggest that a stop to this wastage of resources in the public service should be made now.
However, I want to return to my opening theme, the fiscal incompetence and the financial and economic mismanagement by this administration in general and by the Treasury Board in particular. It has been suggested that a new budget before the end of the year may be required and would be the solution-new taxes, new restraints, something new instead of the old fashioned virtue of thrift. Mark you well, sir, a new budget would mean three budgets in less than 12 months. No wonder there are difficulties when the public and the financial community are subjected to such uncertainties, to so frequent changes of course and pace. What this country needs is not a new budget but a new government.

Mr. Chairman, it is obvious that we are going to have a very interesting discussion of the estimates of the Treasury Board. I want to support the contention that during today's debate the government should take the House of Commons into its confidence and tell us something about its plans so far as financial and fiscal management are

concerned. I think I must also say that during the course of this debate our friends to the right, the members of the official opposition, should zero in and tell us where it is that they think cuts in expenditures should be made. If they are telling us that we should base our financial operations on the basis of priorities, I wish they would come out in the open and give us their list of priorities. I cannot help but have the feeling that the areas in which they would want to save money are precisely those where we think the public has a responsibility, particularly in the fields of health and social welfare. I would feel much happier about the demands of the Progressive Conservatives for cuts in government expenditures if they would pinpoint the places where they think there is waste and in particular if they would have something to say about a department where we feel there is huge over-expenditure, namely, the Department of National Defence.
However, for reasons that I think will be obvious, and taking a position that I am sure would be predictable in every quarter of this house, I wish to spend my few minutes this afternoon on one question, one that the hon. member for Carleton touched upon briefly but effectively. I refer of course to the way in which this government has delayed with respect to increasing the pensions of retired civil servants, including retired R.C.M.P. personnel and retired armed forces personnel.
At the risk of putting on the record something that has been said a good many times but because I think this is the day when we should get an answer from the President of the Treasury Board, may I point out that this subject has been under discussion for a great many years, indeed for well over 20 years to my own knowledge. May I also point out that the President of the Treasury Board ever since June of 1966 has made it quite clear that he is in sympathy with our demands for an increase in the pensions of retired civil servants. He has been good enough to make this clear in private conversation, but everything he has said in private conversation he has said publicly.
It all started in June of 1966 when the President of the Treasury Board expressed his personal willingness to have the matter referred to last session's special joint committee on the public service of Canada. He indicated of course that he would have to get the approval of his colleagues in the government before that reference could be made. He received that approval and the reference was

made in January of 1967. I insist that the reference of that question by the government after six or seven months of consideration was a clear indication to the members of the House of Commons and to our retired civil servants that they could count on something being done if that committee came up with a reasonable recommendation.
The committee spent many meetings in the early part of this year going over this problem. We had excellent chairmen in the person of my good friend, the hon. member for Ottawa East, and our good friend from the other place Senator Bourget. The result of our deliberations was that we came up with a unanimous report. Let me emphasize again that all parties and both houses were represented on that committee, and it came up with a unanimous recommendation that increases in the pensions of the three groups to which we have made reference should be made forthwith.
Since that time we have had a succession of assurances by the President of the Treasury Board and by the Prime Minister that this matter is under active consideration by the cabinet. I have the questions and answers here on my desk, but it is hardly necessary to put them on the record again. No one would deny the fact that we have been told the matter is still on the agenda of the cabinet and is still under active consideration. We have been told that a decision would be made soon. In fact we have been given every right to believe that this issue had some importance in the eyes of the government. But despite the fact that we have had all this consideration, nothing has been done.
Hon. members will recall that the report of the committee was made on May 8 of this year, the last day of the old session, and that some of us had hoped and indeed were led to believe that we would get action on it before we broke for the summer recess. We were disappointed in this hope. When during the first week of July and in particular of July 7, the last day before the recess, I pressed for action before we broke the assurance was given from the other side that this was a matter which could not be dealt with then but in very guarded words it was indicated to us we would get action in the fall.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)

I should like to put in a word to other members of the house, particularly some of those who spoke to me outside the house on July 7 asking me why I was so impatient. There is involved in this whole matter the word of the government, the integrity of the democratic, parliamentary process. I suggest that for the Prime Minister of the country and for the President of the Treasury Board to give the impression something was going to be done and then to disappoint these people is a disservice not only to the people themselves but to the whole parliamentary process. One thing that is necessary if the parliamentary process is going to work is integrity, keeping your word. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that has not been done in this case.
It is very nice to learn from the lips of the President of the Treasury Board that the matter is still on the cabinet agenda, and that as yet a negative decision has not been taken. However, this subject can remain on the cabinet agenda indefinitely with nothing being done for these people. So, Mr. Chairman, I insist that on this day, before we conclude discussion of these estimates, we should have a full statement from the minister that action is going to be taken, not at the end of the session, not next year, but right away.
I do not believe we need to go into a long argument to justify an increase in the pensions of retired civil servants. The justification for such action is set out in the report of the committee that was filed on May 8. The hon. member for Carleton has added to it in the remarks he has just made. The only argument ever put forward against such action is something like this: If we are going to do it for these people, then it may have to be done for others. Well, I agree. As a matter of fact, I feel this is one of the most important questions with which we are going to have to deal in the whole pension field. The government has begun to move in that direction just a little. It has one eye slightly opened down at one corner. The

Supply-Treasury Board government has accepted the principle of the escalation of pensions under the Old Age Security Act and under the Canada Pension Plan. It is a rather miniscule escalation people are going to get in January, 1968, but at least the principle has been recognized. I submit the time will come when all pension arrangements will have to include escalation after pensions are put in pay.
A great many people in this country have learned from experience that what looked like a decent pension when they were five or ten years away from retirement, what might even have looked like a decent pension when they went on retirement, was not much to live on five or ten years after retirement. If we are going to maintain the value of the pension principle, if we are going to support the general idea that people in retirement who helped to build up the country have a right to share in what has been built up, we are going to have to go for pension escalation across the board. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the place for the government to start is with its own employees.
As the hon. member for Carleton pointed out, other jurisdictions have done this. It has been done by most, if not all, provincial governments. It has been done by a number of municipal governments and it has been done in other countries. There is no valid argument against taking this course and taking it now.
One of the things that we, as members of parliament, often would like to be able to do is to listen in on cabinet meetings. This is an opportunity we do not get. Do I see the President of the Treasury Board inviting us to attend some of these meetings?

I believe that when this subject comes up there must be some pretty strong opposition. I do not mean opposition in terms of a great many cabinet ministers because the only two who have spoken out on the issue have been the President of the Treasury Board and the Prime Minister. Both of them have said they are in favour of it. It is my guess, therefore, that the opposition comes from somebody like the Minister of Finance. This is really no secret because he never was partial to it. I suspect that last spring the Minister of Finance was able to persuade his colleagues to put the matter off until fall just by arguing against hasty action. Now he is using the so-called financial
IMr. Knowles.]
crisis, which he denies but which everybody knows is upon us, as an excuse. He says, we cannot spend money here, we cannot spend money there, so we cannot spend money on these people either.
I find it quite immoral, Mr. Chairman, for a minister to take that position. If he is faced with a financial crisis and he has to be concerned with saving hundreds of millions of dollars, then it is immoral to decide that the people who must suffer will be the little people like our own retired employees living on pensions that they had reason to believe would provide them with a decent living in their retirement. The value of these pensions has been so eroded the people are having great difficulty in getting along.
So, Mr. Chairman, I suspect my guess is not far off, that it is the Minister of Finance who is holding things up, who is making it impossible for the cabinet to give a favourable decision on this question. However, this does not excuse the President of the Treasury Board. After all, this matter does corhe under his ministerial responsibility. The item in the estimates covering the superannuation account is in the estimates of the Treasury Board. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the President of the Treasury Board having agreed to let this matter be referred to a committee, having given us the assurance the committees' report was being studied, having told us that the matter is on the cabinet agenda and that he has made proposals to cabinet, has a responsibility to get the matter through cabinet or to take the blame himself for having disillusioned and disappointed the 45,000 or more civil servants and their widows, plus the retired R.C.M.P. personnel, plus the retired armed forces personnel.
I submit that unless he is able to get action he is the person who has to take the final responsibility for getting nothing done. He is a very nice fellow. I forget the adjective the hon. member for Carleton used to describe him, but I will go along with it like other hon. members, I like him. He is genial, very easy to talk to about these matters. He answers our questions on the floor of the house. But when it comes down to this issue, niceness and geniality do not count; what matters is the goods one delivers.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, because the President of the Treasury Board has not yet delivered on this issue, because I believe it is so extremely important not only to the people concerned but to all our people, especially to the people who realize that pensions must be escalated, the people who realize that your

The member for Winnipeg North Centre said: When the time comes for action, the minister gets flustered.
Mr. Chairman, every member of this house would like to obtain the most for his riding, everyone agrees, but it is up to the Treasury Board to decide. For instance, when we ask for the construction of wharves or federal buildings, priorities come into play and it is up to the Treasury Board to distribute the proceeds of taxes levied by the government, income tax, corporate tax or various other sources of taxation. It is a fact that the Treasury Board administers the country in conjunction with the government. And it is according to the amount of taxes collected that the government decides about such and such a project.
For instance, we have heard the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) maintain at one time that the Canadian people were living beyond their means. What do the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) or the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Benson) mean by "living above their means"? And that leads to the present situation where public works, construction, the country's economic growth and the development of its vast resources are slowed down.
We witness for instance the laying off of C.N.R. employees with 15, 17 and even 20 years of service; they were dismissed barely four days ago. They will lose their jobs, as of tomorrow, November 1. Why? It is alleged that there has been a reduction in the use of freight trains. Well, I dare the government to prove there has been a reduction in the use of C.N.R. freight trains in my area. None has occurred. Yet, 22 employees will lose their jobs tonight. Tomorrow, on November 1, these men will no longer be employed with the C.N.R. Why? Because the C.N.R. wants to cut expenses.
People live beyond their means, according to the Minister of Finance. So, let us discontinue all the services, let us prevent, as I said earlier, the normal economic development of our country, let us shrink down every department to the barest minimum, and we shall create a national problem that nobody wants.
Why this situation? Precisely because the Department of Finance, inspired by Treasury Board and the government, is caught in the system which has created this state of affairs.
I wish to call the attention of the minister concerned, the President of the Treasury Board, to the fact that this year our national product is expected to reach $65 billion, and

Supply*-Treasury Board that this compares with a total national revenue expected to reach approximately $47 billion, which makes a difference of $18 billion between the Canadian national product and the Canadian national revenue. And then the minister will say that we are living beyond our means.

But to realize that we have the physical means, the tangible means, in short, the real means, all we have to do is pay a visit to the various business firms and industries in Canada. At this time, industries are cutting production because they are unable to find buyers. Let us go on a tour of the stores and warehouses; they are bursting with goods but, faced with this real abundance, we see the array of financial restrictions imposed on the whole population by the Treasury Board.
The stores inventories are the highest ever. But the people are unable to buy because they do not have the buying power, and the government has announced a "mini budget" to increase taxes. Why? The President of the Treasury Board admits it, the government only administers taxes and can operate only inasmuch as taxes are collected.
If we were concerned with a municipality, I admit that the question might be discussed more seriously. The same would be true if a province were involved, because a province has no monetary powers. They have taxation powers, but there is a world of difference between monetary power and taxation power. The province is helpless. But to have a sovereign government called the government of Canada content to administer through tax collection, Mr. Chairman, that is beyond understanding.
Who has such absolute control of credit beyond the government? Who has more power than the government? We saw it during consideration of the Bank Act last spring when parliament decided to reduce the bank reserves from 8 to 6 per cent, enabling the banking system immediately to create $4 billion in additional credit without a single cent of additional reserve.
The minister is aware that the situation in which we are living may still hold for some time but that it cannot hold forever. The minister also is aware that when the Canadian government issues a million dollars in bonds, the Bank of Canada buys them and, from that moment, the chartered banks have the power to create immediately a $14 million credit for every million in government bonds.
[Mr. Caouette.l
The government borrows from the banks instead of taking its credit at the very source, that is, from the Bank of Canada. The power to control the whole Canadian economic system is given to a few individuals and these individuals, this year, bill us for a debt on which the interest alone will reach the sum of $1,273,906,400. This represents a slight increase of $88,417,500 from last year, and federal members swallow it. Nobody rises to tell the President of the Treasury Board: Cut down the interest we are paying on the debt. No. Let us rather bear down on the pockets of miners, settlers, on the little Canadian worker. Bear down and crush him, but let us show respect and veneration for the interest on the national debt created out of nothing by a handful of individuals.
Mr. Chairman, the interests on the national debt only have increased by $88 million. Nobody complains, nobody disagrees. But the people are subject to restrictions. It is strange that no minister, no government member rises to protest against that outright theft, the interest on the national debt. And none of them protest against the restrictions and the control of priorities by the Treasury Board that the government is about to lay upon us in a few weeks by means of a mini-budget. On the other hand, that same Treasury Board will cost the Canadian people $183,908,000 this year or $40 million more than last year. Nobody objects to that. We find normal that the government should spend right and left, while failing to face realities in our country. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was talking earlier about pensions and social security. Nobody is against those things. On the contrary, we are all in favour of the most elaborate, adequate and satisfactory form of social security for the whole population.
But nobody asks, for instance, where will we get the money for that. That is the problem. Everybody is willing to grant a pension to our old or needy people, to increase civil service salaries. Everybody wants it, but our financial system does not allow it. Instead of thinking in terms of physical possibilities we have in Canada to develop our resources and produce even greater wealth, we are thinking in terms of dollars.
Our administration depends on the revenues we get from taxation. What a lovely sovereignty for a government which calls itself sovereign. Is it sovereignty to have to kneel before financiers and ask their permission to grant a pension, to raise social security or to increase civil service salaries?

Mr. Chairman, nobody is opposed to these raises but, there again, has the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre told us of which department he would like to see the expenditures drastically reduced in order to allow for the salary increase? Could the hon. member for Carleton tell us later on to what department the government should go to get the funds for one priority or another? Neither of them suggests a solution.
Mr. Chairman, when we suggest a solution -because the Creditistes have one which they have advocated now for thirty-five years-some still attempt to ridicule it rather than try to understand it. Quite often we give them conspicuous examples. If the war were to break out tomorrow, do you think that those restrictions would exist? Of course not. We would then call upon the Bank of Canada to set up war plants all across Canada. There would be no question of any lack of funds. But, for peace, for the security of our fellow citizens, for the safety of the Canadian people, it is immediately a monetary problem and nothing else but that.
Mr. Chairman, what have we been suggesting for a long time? That the whole public sector be financed directly by the Bank of Canada, that a branch of the Bank of Canada be established in every Canadian province so that each one may look after its own administration according to its possibilities, its aspirations, its physical possibilities. And then we would no longer hear anything about separatism or independence, hatred among ourselves in Canada. The whole question of separatism, so topical in Canada today, is due to nothing but an economic, financial and even monetary situation.
That is where the problem lies and everyone will recognize it. In fact, it is the No. 1 problem in any riding but also at the provincial level, and it is so real that the premier of Ontario, Mr. Robarts, said in London two days ago that the discussion at the interprovincial conference on constitutional matters, which will be held in Toronto in the latter part of November, would boil down to a matter of dollars and cents for each of the provinces. Those are not my words, they are those of Mr. Robarts, the premier of Ontario. Are we beginning to open our eyes or are we simply talking through our hat? Are we afraid to deal with the problem, to get to the bottom of the matter, in short, to do as suggested by the great French general: Let us get to the bottom of things.

People are afraid of separatism, of inde-pendentists, of this hatred arising between various parts of Canada at this time, but when one travels throughout Canada, one sees that the same problem is facing us everywhere, that is to say, in all the provinces, there are poor people in the midst of affluence. These points are not dealt with on radio, on television, in the press, Mr. Chairman. No. The financial manipulations of the country must be hushed up.

Those who would cast light on the shameless exploitation of the financial system must be hushed up. Well, let it be hushed up. Such organized and systematic silences have bred revolutions in European countries. To avoid revolution here in Canada, on our Canadian soil, it is high time that we face the problem, not shy away from it, and accept a sensible solution which will, at long last, enable the Canadian people to unite, to see the whole of the country and to realize the wealth it owns. Nowadays, because people are growing less aware of their wealth, they rise against each other. As far as the financial question is concerned, the federal government lacks the courage to settle it, to bring finance in step with reality and have it serve the Canadian people.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to speak this afternoon on one particular issue. In beginning my remarks, however, I should like to say that if the Canadian people ever had any faith in the ability of the present government to administer in an effective way the monetary and fiscal policy which Canada requires, that faith is being rapidly undermined. The actions of the government have shown clearly that it is either unaware of the effect of its policies on the national economy or that it is struggling vainly and desperately to find an answer to problems which are too great for it to tackle.
I do not intend this afternoon to discuss the whole realm of monetary and fiscal policy. I think the views of this party were put in clear perspective at the time the banking legislation was before us and I shall not repeat the arguments which were used then. However, I believe the time has come for the government to take a realistic view of the economic situation and that instead of continuing to follow old programs and policies which have been tried over and over again and proven futile it should be bold and adventurous enough to try something different.
I recall speaking to a supporter of the government some years ago about monetary

and fiscal policy. He said: "We all know that the present system is not satisfactory or adequate to meet modern needs but I am not confident yet that you people have the right answers." So we are suggesting now that the minister and the government be bold enough to try something different. Even if it does not work 100 per cent as anticipated, such a plan, provided it brings advantages to the Canadian people, would be a step in the right direction.
I indicated when I began that it was my intention to deal with one particular matter this afternoon. It is one which has already been raised by the hon. member for Carleton and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre-the attitude of the Treasury Board and the government in relation to superannuated federal civil servants. A review of the record will show how often this question has been raised in the house and the many occasions upon which the President of the Treasury Board has indicated that the subject was receiving active consideration. It reminds us of what is said by the Minister of Veterans Affairs when we call attention to the need for increases in disability pensions, war veterans allowances and so on. He always said that the government is giving careful consideration to these matters, but so far nothing concrete has been done.
Similarly, nothing concrete has been done with respect to the pensions of superannuated civil servants despite all the recommendations which have been made and all the arguments which have been advanced in the house. I was a member of the public service committee while this question was before it for consideration. At that time there was general agreement that something ought to be done to increase these pensions. I do not recall even the government members on the committee raising any particular objection or questioning the desirability of increasing the pensions of superannuated civil servants. Perhaps I was naive, but I was of the opinion that after the tabling of our recommendations we could look forward to early action on this matter. However, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, we have waited and waited in vain. Even now we have no indication whatsoever that favourable consideration is going to be given to this matter.

It is not necessary to present all the arguments in favour of such an increase. The

minister knows them very well. The government knows them very well. Each hon. member is well aware of the reasons why consideration should and must be given to this matter. Therefore I do not think anything will be gained by repetition of those arguments today. During the course of the debate on the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs I said that if the government was considering economies I did not think it proper that those who had served in our armed forces should be called upon to bear the brunt of those economies. The main purpose of parliament is the voting of supply, and on this there must be no equivocation. However, finding some inspiration in what I think is a misguided view of the Glassco commission of the functions and purposes of parliament, newspaper writers, commentators and other people have started to worship at the altar of that great god efficiency. They say we must tidy things up. We must make the parliamentary process slick and work like the board of a tightly knit, smoothly operating corporation. To those people I would comment-as a matter of fact I say it should be required reading -volume No. 28 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the public accounts committee of November 23 last, and in particular the testimony of the Auditor General.
The Auditor General is not a servant of the government. He is responsible to this house and-

-and there is no question in my mind that the Auditor General is responsible to parliament. I make that assertion knowing full well that there may be some opposite who will not share it and it may not even be shared by some of the gentlemen who work for the Treasury Board and whose personal abilities and capabilities I respect. But this spirit has grown up in the Treasury Board, as in the cabinet, that it and it alone shall have the control. That must not be the case.
As an example I would refer to the form of the estimates themselves. In 1963-64 there was a great consolidation of titles of estimates, presumably for the sake of efficiency. For example, under the present form of the estimates over 80 per cent of the expenditures of the Department of National Defence appear under one vote. We believe that parliament does have control, but by the proposed step we are giving the ministry a blank cheque. The same applies to other departments.
What has happened to the salary item under the Department of Finance, which is now contained within a contingency item in the Treasury Board estimates? In its present form it is asking the house to give the cabinet and the Treasury Board a blank cheque in order to get away from control of expenditures by parliament.

I feel that such a transfer would be wrong both for the government and for the opposition. In this way there might come a time when the government would use this lever, which is in effect a blackjack, to force the opposition to allow interim supply in order to pay the salaries of public servants who are the innocent parties in such a struggle. I shall conclude by saying what I think is the purpose of the Treasury Board. Mr. Chairman, not only in respect of the discussion of these estimates but also on many other occasions since this house reconvened a number of weeks ago members from all parties on this side of the house have stated time and time again that because of the government's ill-timed fiscal and monetary policies it has consistently destroyed many of the options open to it to move the economy of Canada forward as it should be moved forward at the present time. Nowhere is this statement more true than in relation to what is happening in the Treasury Board under the present minister at this time. Canadians have been told, through a series of leaks planned or otherwise, that the present government is now advocating a number of major cuts in expenditures. I do not intend to argue about this. I believe the present administration will find much agreement on this side of the house and from the people of Canada that major cuts are necessary at the present time.
Tell us where. Which cuts?

I do not think that is necessary. I do not have any specific cuts in mind at the present time. We will hear the hon. member in due course when he takes part in this debate. I again repeat that it is apparent that major cuts are in order at the present time and apparently are being made. Most members of this house and many Canadians are asking why there is a necessity for wholesale cuts at the present time. They are asking why this disorganization has arisen which has necessitated this activity by the Treasury Board.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
I shall not preface my very brief and general remarks on priorities with any notion that government per se is just business, big or otherwise. Far too many people when discussing governmental activities say that government should be run like a big business. I do not agree with this, although I do agree that we need more business attitudes in the running of government day to day. The main question that I want to put briefly this afternoon, one that has already been mentioned, is: What is the reason for this cutting back activity by the Treasury Board at the present time? The simple reason is that the present administration is guilty of a lack of long term or even medium term thinking about where this country is going and how its economy should be planned. How else could the government have found itself in the mess it is in today? Is it the result of long term or medium term planning? Of course not. It is the result of a leaderless, rudderless government going from crisis to crisis. I am sure the hon. lady knows what I am talking about. She has been looking for a president for the C.B.C. for a year now. That is not the result of long term planning.
Ask the Prime Minister about it. I have nothing to do with it.

The hon. lady is blaming the Prime Minister. He will probably blame her. The surprising thing about this government is that in their state of inactivity they blame everyone but themselves. The fact is that the chaos in the Treasury Board today is the result of a lack of long or medium term economic planning. It is also the result of the government's refusal to allocate priorities in the economic and social fields.

Mr. Chairman, I must confess I am a little confused in trying to ascertain what the position of the official opposition is with regard to government cuts, about which I have read in the newspapers. So far as one can determine from the last speaker for the official opposition, the Conservative party hopes the government will put on the brake and drive straight ahead with a foot on the accelerator. This is not usually considered a good method of driving.
Sometimes I am reminded of my long political career. Years ago, before many members of this house were born or were very old, I entered the legislature of British Columbia. At that time I thought, now I am really going to see the cream of the province of British Columbia, the real brains; they have to be here. I am going to see someone who will enlighten and impress me tremendously. I still remember the great shock that overcame me when I began to realize there was no one there any brighter than I was, and I was not very bright.
Was it worse when you came here?

I thought when I came here I was coming to the centre of information. Surely I was going to meet the really bright, intellectual lights of this country. I was ready to take a properly humble attitude toward these people whose names I had been reading in the newspapers all my life. They must be men of tremendous capacity. Again, I had the disconcerting experience of realizing that one after the other of these people I was prepared to set up as idols had feet of clay. They revealed that they were little, if any, brighter than I was, and again I admit that I
October 31, 1967

am not very bright. This was very disconcerting.
There was one person we used to hear about continually, but I had not met him. His name used to crop up all the time but he was almost a mysterious personage. His name popped up everywhere as the ultimate in competence, a man who really knew how to make the economy work, a man who had made it work during the war as one of C. H. Howe's boys. Here was a man who would finally put things on an even keel after the rather bad start that this government had had and the rather distressing experience of the previous government. Finally, of course, this mysterious personage emerged as the present Minister of Finance.
Again, I must confess to a feeling of considerable dismay because I believed the stories that here was competence incarnate. Well, we have to admit that today things are in a very bad mess. Even Peter Newman has had to wash his hands of the Liberal party and the Liberal government. Peter has really been a faithful apologist for this government. Admittedly he has had many disappointments as a great many of his idols have suddenly revealed their clay feet. Only recently has Peter finally thrown up his hands and said that the government is in a mess and does not know what it is doing. There is no doubt about it, things are in a mess.
It is all very well for the Minister of Finance to tell us, as he told us today in answer to a question of mine, that there is no such thing as a money crisis. I was quoting from a report of his speech in Montreal. I do not know whether he used that term in Montreal, but certainly he conveyed the impression to his audience that he considered there was something that could be termed a money crisis. This is a very bad expression, I admit, and one that rather offends my pedantic nature. However, we all know what is meant. Things are in very bad mess financially in Canada.
Our friends in the official opposition appear to think that the financial and economic troubles we are experiencing are caused solely by governmental extravagance. I have no dobut whatever that there is a great deal of governmental extravagance, a great deal of governmental waste. I submit, however, that this cannot be the real cause of the troubles that are now overtaking the Canadian economy.
In the first place, I feel we should be careful not to draw such sharp distinctions
Supply-Treasury Board between public and private expenditures. They all come out of the same stream of wealth production. It is when you try to spend that wealth in the two places at once that you get into trouble. It is when you try to build the unnecessary sort of buildings that have been undertaken in Canada and at the same time have the government perform the necessary social services it has to look after that you begin to run into trouble. It is when the capital of the country is allowed to behave as it wishes, without any control from the central authorities, that we begin to run into trouble.
We are told almost ad nauseam, and have been for some years, how dependent we are on foreign capital coming into this country to keep our economy on an even keel and to enable us to expand. However, I have two reports here which indicate what has been happening to the Canadian economy and provide an answer to the questions I have been putting to a number of my economist friends who try to tell me our troubles have arisen because our level of investment has been falling. When I suggest to them this is a nonsensical, meaningless statement because investment cannot fall as long as the total money supply is expanding, they retreat muttering in their beards.
It may be that investment is not taking place in the spots in which they are accustomed to finding it. I suggest what we are seeing today is a flight of capital from Canada. This flight of capital in no way differs from other flights of capital in the past and is caused perhaps by the same reasons that have caused flights of capital in earlier times and in other countries. One of the reasons in this country has been that the government simply refuses to control and direct the economy.
There has been a sharp rise in the volume of Canadian trading on the Chicago and midwest stock exchange. Very interesting figures are contained in a report in today's Globs and Mail. These figures indicate that the transactions of Canadian stock brokerage firms who hold seats on this exchange rose from $58 million in 1966 to $325 million this year. These figures indicate where a lot of Canadian capital is going and it has to be replaced, of course, by importation of capital. Then we have the Gazette stating quite
October 31, 1967

Supply-Treasury Board unequivocally that there has been a flight of capital from Canada.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
In a country already capital-hungry, the need will be intense. Will the capital be found?
It is unlikely to be found until Canada is able to present to Canadians and to the world a more confident outlook. The fact is that Canadian money is itself moving out of the country in enormous amounts, to seek more attractive opportunities for investment elsewhere.
This is an astonishing editorial comment, Mr. Chairman, when one realizes the level of interest rates in Canada. One can only assume it is a profound disquiet over the manner in which the government of Canada has been conducting our affairs that causes these funds to be flowing out of the country. I was warned some months ago by a man in a position to know that there was a serious flight of capital taking place via mutual open-end funds from Canada into the United States, and I presume that this is another example of that same tendency.
This is posing problems for us, Mr. Chairman, that the government is refusing to meet. Not long ago I asked the Minister of Finance whether he did not think that two policies to which this government is committed are mutually incompatible. One policy is the maintenance of a fixed exchange rate and the other is the maintenance of the $2,600 million maximum reserve that we have agreed to keep in our agreement with the United States. My question was prompted by a news item that the Bank of Canada had been obliged to get into the market in order to drive down the value of the Canadian dollar to the pegged level of 92.5 cents United States. It had been pushed up, of course, by the inflow of capital which we are repeatedly told is necessary in order to keep Canada going and to keep Canada expanding.
I am going to suggest, Mr. Chairman, that it is useless to belabour this government, as has been done from the official opposition benches, on the ground that they have brought troubles upon us by their extravagance and not to point out that the cure for these troubles lies much deeper than that. It lies in the fact that the government will not control the operations of our economy. I suggest that before long the Minister of Finance is going to have to make a choice. He is going to have to go to the International Monetary Fund and negotiate us back into a floating exchange rate or he is going to have to abandon the agreement with the United States to maintain only a maximum of $2,600 
million in American funds in our exchange reserves. The two policies are incompatible and they are becoming daily more and more incompatible.
Whether the government is prepared to do that is another matter, Mr. Chairman. I would doubt that they are. I think we shall flounder along and probably the government will adopt, as the minister has hinted thus far that it will adopt, the crude method of turning the screws on the economy, allowing unemployment to rise, so as to overcome for the time being the problems that the government is facing. We certainly will not solve these problems by severe government cuts which are not compensated for elsewhere in the economy.
I can see a place where there could be a cut, Mr. Chairman, and I should like to ask my Conservative friends where they would cut. I can tell you where I would cut. I would cut the defence expenditures. It is 14 years since I first sat in this house and every year since then the government of Canada has spent $1,500 million, $1,600 million, $1,700 million on so-called military defence. No minister of national defence and no government spokesman has ever been able to tell me what defence has been achieved for Canada by these expenditures. So I have no hesitation in saying that I would make cuts there if I thought cuts had to be made.
Even so, Mr. Chairman, I would not make cuts and leave it at that. I would transfer those expenditures to other fields which would develop the Canadian economy in a way in which we can continue to advance, expand and develop. But we are not going to do this merely by turning the screw now in a crude, undifferentiated and unselective way, or by going to departments, as the government is doing at the present moment according to the spokesman of the Conservative party who appears to know-I do not-and whittling a few million off here and a few million off there. All we do by that method is to further the decline in the Canadian economy and increase the problems of the Canadian people.
I hope the government will eventually realize that there is no distinction that can properly be made in an industrial economy between public expenditures and private expenditures, that it is a case of deciding what is best for the Canadian people. Those on the government benches tell us, of course, that they are helpless in the hands of our constitution. We have had pointed out to us several times that provincial and municipal
October 31, 1967

expenditures have been rising above federal expenditures, which I think they did for the first time last year or perhaps the year before. That is perfectly true. But I also suggest that any federal government worthy of the name can reach agreements with the provincial governments without too much difficulty. The fact is that provincial governments are obliged to make their policies conform to those of the federal government if the federal government wishes to ensure that outcome.
I have yet to see this government or any other federal government deal with the problem of reaching agreements with the provincial governments by advertising to the people of the provinces the answers that the federal government has to obstacles that may be put in their way by the provincial governments and thus bring provincial governments to the frame of mind which will induce them to co-operate with the federal government. These things, I am sure, can be done if we have a government that is prepared to govern. And to govern today means more than just holding the ring as a referee; it means direct participation in the economy of the country.
In a news item the other day there was a hint that the legislation relating to the Canada Development Corporation, if and when it comes before us, will be of a very different type from that envisaged by the former minister of finance. His concept of it, you remember, Mr. Chairman, was a sort of vast mutual fund which was to be used for purchasing back minority shares of foreign-owned corporations. The news item to which I refer, which had all the earmarks of an inspired leak, was that the present Minister of Finance has in mind using the funds of the Canada Development Corporation for that sort of rationalization and regrouping of Canadian industry that the members of this industry have been pressing upon him now for a year and a half.
I hope that this is the plan and that it goes beyond the sort of guide lines and pleadings that he suggests in his dealings with the rest of the economy. I hope that this means government participation and intervention in developing and controlling the Canadian economy. If our government will do that, Mr. Chairman, I think we shall no longer have the trouble we presently have of capital shortages, of continually increasing interest rates, of a rising consumer price index, of declining production, of a declining gross
Supply-Treasury Board national product or rate or growth in Canada. We shall go ahead in the way in which anyone with any common sense realizes that this country can go ahead.
I say this because there are few people on the face of the earth so fortunate as the Canadian people, with resources that are unmatched anywhere on the globe. If we fail to take advantage of these opportunities in Canada to produce a society that will be an example for the rest of the world, then we should be thoroughly ashamed of having elected such an incompetent government.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I hope our Minister of Finance will realize this is an opportunity. I hope that for him this is not merely an unfortunate situation in which he finds himself without knowing how he got into it. I hope he and his colleagues are prepared to do the sort of thing that a modern government in a modern industrial society must do if democratic government is to survive in an industrial age.

The amendment is the only means available to us to express our dissatisfaction with the government's failure to take action with regard to retired civil servants and others who have been waiting patiently for the implementation of a certain report. Other hon. members have mentioned the ill effects of the stringent allocation of time for estimates. I have spoken on this subject on many occasions. At this time I believe that the mistake in setting a 30 day limit on the discussion of estimates has been brought home to all members of the house. We are facing a financial crisis which can most usefully be discussed on the estimates of the Treasury Board and those of the Department of Finance. Yet the limitation imposed on the house means that we have only another two and a half hours left today for the discussion of these major matters and the time that will be available on Thursday. Then the guillotine will operate and millions of dollars will be voted without a full discussion of whether it is advisable that this money should be spent.

speechtext: It is hundreds of millions of dollars.

The hon. member says that the amount will run to hundreds of millions of dollars. I do not know. The total may be in the billions of dollars. This demonstrates the weakness of setting a time limit for the study of estimates, especially such a short time limit as 30 days. As other members have said, no subject is of greater importance to the House of Commons than the financial aspects of government. During the last two years these financial aspects have, unfortunately, been shoved into the background. Estimates have been taken on a hit or miss basis; sometimes they have been postponed. Year after year we have voted interim supply so that expenditures may be maintained.
The last time you were in office you did not call them at all.
The estimates have not been subjected to the careful and close scrutiny they should have. Ministers of the crown have not been called on to defend their policies.
The minister is in the house for one day and has a lot to answer for.

Ministers have not delineated their policies. We saw an example of that sort of thing last night. The Minister of Industry failed to return to the house at eight o'clock even though his estimates were before the committee. The chairman thought that the committee was still dealing with the Department of Industry and called for the passing of item No. 1. The hon. member for Carleton properly objected. Then we had a change of business; we took up the Department of Public Works. The estimates of the Minister of Industry may not come before the committee again. Without any answers from him his estimates will go through. The guillotine will operate. The steam roller on the government side of the house will cooperate to push items through.
We talk about reforming parliament. Over the years one of the reforms advocated was shortening the time for the discussion of estimates. I and other hon. members of this party opposed that concept from the beginning. The idea was tried on a trial basis and we have been operating under the concept of limitation of time for discussion of estimates for two or three years. The idea is a complete failure. What has happened this year has shown it up in its stark reality. I am sure that members of the combined opposition will oppose making permanent the temporary rule that set a limit of 30 days for the study of estimates.
Several speakers outlined in considerable detail and with eloquence the financial troubles of this country. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands said that we were placing too much stress on cutting back expenditures. I hope he approves of the suggestion to cut back reckless expenditures. That is not our only argument. It is one that we have been stressing today and we have stressed it for a simple reason. During the last three months we have had indications from the Prime Minister's office and elsewhere that great reductions in expenditures were to be made. It was said that hundreds of millions of dollars were do be cut from expenditures. Anyone who has been in the house for any length of time, and certainly anyone who has served on the government

side, knows perfectly well that is the phoniest, yes, the phoniest cutting back of expenditures that we have ever heard of.
Hear, hear.
