subtopic: COMMERCIAL SOLIDS PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I recall I had been speaking for about two minutes when the time ran out on the last occasion that this bill was before the house. It seems to me that in our centennial year it is very appropriate to recall some of our Canadian history for the purpose of giving us some guide lines for the future in the field of transportation. As I am sure every member of the house recalls from his study of our history, it is about 80 years ago that a transcontinental railroad was finally built across Canada which bound together the various parts of this country. This was a tremendous undertaking and one that was absolutely necessary if Canada was to emerge as a national entity. It was the means by which the very diverse parts of this enormous country could be welded together. One could not expect that at that period the railroad would be constructed in any way except by private enterprise or that the benefits of constructing it would accrue to anybody but private citizens or groups of private citizens. At that time the concept of social and communal rights was rather undeveloped.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
After the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway there was a spate of railway construction in various regions of the country which culminated, as I recall, in 1912 with the construction of the line to Prince Rupert on the Pacific coast in the constituency of my hon. friend from Skeena. Many members will recall the sad history of that vast railway construction period in our Canadian history. They will recall how grafting contractors, corrupt governments and greedy individuals and groups contributed to what became almost a national disaster which necessitated the government of Canada moving into the picture and cobbling together all the various ill-fated railway projects which had been constructed without any hope of an economically sound future.
We have not yet recovered from the results of that particular page in our history. Almost every year one hears complaints in the house about the cost of Canadian National Railways which was the result of the government taking over these bankrupt railway projects that had been built in that expansionary period. We still are paying the cost of allowing private interests to move into a field on which the whole of our economy rested, the field of transport upon which our whole national economy relied and depended. We allowed it to be the happy hunting ground

for those who wanted to make profits from the development of the new Dominion of Canada. I suggest that this burden has been too hard on the Canadian people and it is only now that we are beginning to get on top of it.
For many years it has been pointed out that the government's action at that time, while in some ways commendable, was also very badly contrived because of its position that the best thing to do was to allow certain groups in our economy to profit from the operation of the economy. Therefore, instead of allowing these concerns to go bankrupt, instead of allowing their bonds to drop out of sight, the government of Canada on behalf of the taxpayers of Canada guaranteed them, and from that day to this we have been carrying a very heavy burden.
We are now moving into a new age with new methods of transportation. Perhaps the most striking and significant is the one outlined in Bill C-113, to incorporate the Commercial Solids Pipe Line Company. The purpose is to transport by modern methods commodities that hitherto have been transported by railroad or water and perhaps to a minor degree in recent years by air. In the main it will be commodities carried by railroads that will be transported.
We can be sure that technological advances will improve the scope, capacity and ability of these pipe lines to transport goods in pelletized or solid form as is now being attempted. I assume there is every anticipation on the part of this company that the operation is going to be very profitable; otherwise it would not have distributed the very expensive brochure I and other members have received from the sponsors of this bill. We can be quite sure that the moment it is demonstrated that pipe lines represent the modern method of transportation and that this is a means by which promoters can make fortunes for themselves, their colleagues and associates, we shall have a spate of pipe line construction as great as the railway construction which occurred 50 to 60 years ago. We may very well experience an even greater disastrous result. It may well be that we will have to come again to the rescue of bankrupt transportation companies because they have built pipe lines as the railroads were built, paralleling each other across this country. In my own province there are two railroads running down the Fraser canyon, one on one side and one on the other, periodically having to hop across
October 31, 1967

Private Bills
and change places before arriving at the same destination, Vancouver.
There has been a scandalous waste of resources so far as the Canadian National is concerned, and of course evidence of that is the very heavy load of debt placed on the Canadian people by the government which decided it had to rescue these bankrupt operators. I plead with the house to be very careful not to permit Canada to embark on another period of wasteful construction of a means of transportation and to realize that in this day and age there is no place in the field of transportation for private interests. This is too important a factor in our economy.
We have seen in recent years the transfer of virtually all electric power production and distribution from private to public hands. We have seen the various utilities across the country falling into public hands because private hands have proved incompetent or incapable of providing the services required. I submit that transportation, particularly transcontinental, which is the means through which our country is tied together, is too important a matter to be left in the hands of private interests or promoters whose concern, quite legitimately and legally, is to make profits by the transportation of goods in Canada.
I hope the house will decide not to pass this bill. I hope the government will thereupon take note of the refusal of the parliament of Canada to embark on what I think is a very misguided project and undertake the sort of research and development which will lead to public investment in a properly integrated pipe line transportation system in Canada. For that reason I move:
That Bill C-113, an act to incorporate Commercial Solids Pipe Line Company, be not now read a second time, but that it be read a second time this day six months hence.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have just seen another example of the kind of action that will result in a refusal to hear people who are anxious to develop Canada's natural resources. I think it is a pity that it is possible for a very limited number of members to hold up that development, particularly in the field of research and transportation, which is so vital to the economic well-being of Canada as a nation. I say this because the passage of Bill C-113, as all hon. members know, would not in fact give any company the right to build a solids pipe line or any other kind of pipe line. Indeed, all it would do is set up a legal entity
which could make application to the Canadian Transportation Commission and thereby have the opportunity to place before the commission its proposal and the economic arguments in favour of it.
If we should at this stage take the action suggested by the amendment the bill would not even be referred to the committee. The sponsors of this company would not have the right to be heard in any forum. I think that would be unjust and unfair. Anyone who has respect for the concept of justice and democratic discussion should at least provide an opportunity to the sponsors to state their case before members of this house. A bill similar to this one has been before the house now for nearly two years without being given second reading. If this bill were given second reading and referred to the committee, the officers of the company could be called before the committee to state their case.
Section 24 of the National Transportation Act which was passed by this house earlier in 1967 provides that subject to subsection 2 no company shall operate a commodity pipe line unless there is a certificate in force with respect to that pipe line. Therefore, even if the bill should pass through all stages in this house this would not permit the Commercial Solids Pipe Line Company to begin immediately construction of a pipe line or go into the pipe line business, in this case the moving of sulphur from Alberta to the west coast.
Other stringent conditions have also been laid down in the new National Transportation Act such as section 25 which provides that the transportation commission before it grants a certificate must study such things as the economic feasibility of the pipe line, the financial responsibility and financial structure of the applicant, the methods of financing the pipe line and the extent to which Canadians will have an opportunity of participating in the financing, engineering and construction of the pipeline, and any public interest that in the opinion of the commission may be affected by the granting or refusing of the application.
The company has already stated there will be a public offering of shares when they have reached the stage in their research where they find that the project is probably economically feasible. That, of course, is not certain at this time. I believe that in Canada we must pay far more attention to the modernization of our transportation industries so that we can remain competitive in international markets in respect of many commodities. Wheat, for

example, is very important but many other raw materials are produced in Canada, such as sulphur, which fall in this category.
In many other countries sulphur is produced much closer to tidewater than it is in Canada. Unless we find a more economical way to move this material from the point where it is produced to the coast we will be participating in the restriction of the expansion of our world markets for sulphur. Sulphur is a product which is basic to industry. It has been said that sulphuric acid is the work horse of the chemical industry. Sulphur is the major and essential ingredient of sulphuric acid. If Canada is to expand its industrial base, both in respect of the production of raw materials and also its secondary industries, sulphur will become one of our most important resources.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I certainly hope that hon. members will not prevent this bill from getting second reading so that it may be referred to the committee where we will have an opportunity to hear from the officers of the company. There will be plenty of time after the committee stage to disagree with the arguments which may be advanced. It seems to me that it will be a very serious miscarriage of justice in so far as this house is concerned if we refuse them the opportunity to state their case to certain members of this house.

Mr. Speaker, on June 20, 1967 when this matter was last considered my colleague from Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) had the floor for a brief moment. I spoke on this bill on second reading, as did other hon. members, and I cannot take the time of the house to go into the intricacies of detail in connection with the company because this would necessitate rereading from Hansard some of the thoughts expressed by the sponsor of the bill, and others who spoke at an earlier stage.
One of the interesting points about Aetna Casualty Company is that it is the subsidiary of a company based in Hartford, Connecticut. Most of its business is conducted in Canada, but the interesting point is that its business of insurance is carried on with companies that are also subsidiaries of United States corporations.
This, Mr. Speaker, is one of the very bad features of a corporate structure such as this, because there is a sort of closed circuit. One company sets up a subsidiary in Canada, owns and controls it and makes decisions with respect to it, whether it be a production company, a distribution company or what have you. These decisions are not based on the worth that may accrue to Canada but are based upon influences which are brought to bear upon the parent company in another country, in this instance in the United States.
This company based in Hartford, Connecticut has been operating in Canada through

October 31, 1967

its subsidiary for some years, and its subsidiary in Canada has been carrying on its business of insurance with other United States subsidiaries. In other words, there has been no involvement whatever in the day to day economic life of Canada; it is simply an engagement to insure items with which other U.S. subsidiaries would be involved.
I have remarked on another occasion what this bill covers in the way of insurance, Mr. Speaker, and perhaps I may be permitted to relate them to these remarks because they form the principal part of the bill. This company wishes to be incorporated to carry on and transact insurance business in the particular fields and classes of fire insurance, accident insurance, aircraft insurance, automobile insurance, boiler insurance, credit insurance, earthquake insurance, explosion insurance, falling aircraft insurance, forgery insurance, guarantee insurance, hail insurance, impact by vehicles insurance, inland transportation insurance, livestock insurance, machinery insurance, marine insurance, personal property insurance, plate glass insurance, real property insurance, sickness insurance, sprinkler leakage insurance, theft insurance, water damage insurance, weather insurance and windstorm insurance.
I have listed 26 classes of insurance coverage which this company is seeking to have authority to sell in Canada. Presumably they are the classes of insurance that the company has been selling up to now, it having been in existence in this country for some 40 or 50 years. You can see from the recitation of the types of insurance, encompassing the alphabet from A to Z, that almost every type of insurance coverage one can think of is included. In other words this company wants to become involved in the whole range of insurance, with the exception of medical coverage insurance, hospital insurance and the like, and life insurance. Every class of insurance relating to real property is, I presume, included here.
The indication is, Mr. Speaker, that this company wants not only to engage in the full range of insurance coverage but wants this range in order that it may carry on its activities of insuring every type of insurance coverage under the sun with only subsidiaries of United States corporations.
The 1965 premium income of Aetna Casualty increased 17 per cent over the year before, to $665 million. This is a fair sized amount of premium income and I am sure represents millions upon millions of dollars

of real property insured, all of it under the cloak of foreign ownership.
We know the position taken by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) on foreign ownership. He told us on a nation-wide television broadcast that he is partial to Canadian ownership. We know what is the position of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Gordon); he has clearly said on many occasions that he is partial to Canadian ownership. There are those in the cabinet who do not disagree in essence with the President of the Privy Council but disagree only about some of his methods. However, they too are partial to the concept of Canadian ownership.
As I have said before on a number of occasions, Mr. Speaker, I think it behooves this parliament to concern itself with Canadian ownership. The Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act requires that companies that sell certain classes of insurance, are newly incorporated and do not have an international connection prior to a certain date, must have the element of Canadian ownership in them that puts majority control in the hands of Canadians. This is the philosophy of the statute law of this parliament as it applies to life insurance companies. The government, through the Prime Minister and others, have clearly said that it is their hope, desire and intention that all companies in Canada will become Canadian owned. To this extent we want to assist in every way we can.
A moment ago, Mr. Speaker, we dealt with a company that fell into this category. We did not touch on the ownership aspect of that matter, but this will arise on another occasion.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
I cannot conceive of this parliament even considering passage of a bill to incorporate a company which is owned and controlled in the United States. The policies of the company are determined by what is valuable for the United States company. The company is to sell insurance only to other subsidiaries of United States owned corporations.
It is bad enough that we are asked to incorporate a company that has shown no interest in becoming Canadian owned, or in being responsible to the Canadian economy and the Canadian society. Yet we are asked to incorporate a company that has not exhibited one iota of interest in becoming Canadian owned; it is to remain exclusively under the control of Aetna Casualty Company of Hartford, Connecticut. This company
October 31, 1967

which seeks incorporation under the aegis of the parliament of Canada will sell its insurance policies only to companies which also are subsidiaries of United States corporations. These subsidiaries in other words will take out insurance policies for any one of the 26 classes of insurance which the company seeking incorporation wishes to sell.
It may be seen that insurance money will be put into the hands of a company which has no direct responsibility to the Canadian economy, in the sense in which other companies that are wholly owned within the nation have responsibility to the economy. It is too much to ask parliament to consider incorporating such company.
Some time ago the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) sent a letter to all such subsidiaries telling them what he thought was involved in good Canadian corporate citizenship-I think that is the term he used. The practice of good Canadian corporate citizenship should not involve, I think, one company being the subsidiary of a second company which sells insurance only to other subsidiaries, thus maintaining a closed circuit so far as money is concerned, with control of the company to be incorporated being retained in the hands of those who live in another nation.
Under such an arrangement insurance premiums paid are directed to a company which is controlled in the United States. I submit that we ought to look at a number of recent precedents that act as guide lines for companies that seek to be incorporated by parliament, or for companies that are subsidiaries of corporations of other nations. One example is that of the Mercantile Bank. I shall not go into details, but here was a situation in which the government of Canada expressed itself firmly and with determination with respect to the matter of Canadian versus foreign ownership, requiring Mercantile Bank within a certain period to comply with the rules of the game, so far as Canada was concerned.
Another precedent was that of United Investment Life Assurance Company, which was a subsidiary of a United States corporation. United Investment came before parliament seeking incorporation. After that company ran into the obstacle of being questioned about its good Canadian corporate structure and citizenship the parent company voluntarily said that within a certain period-and it is only reasonable that some time should be permitted for this to happen-it
Private Bills
was prepared to divest itself of its ownership of the Canadian subsidiary. Failing that, under Canadian insurance legislation, the shares of that company held in the United States would lose their voting power
In other words, if United Investment Life Assurance Company did not comply with the rules as established for Canadian ownership, the shareholdings in the United States would lose their voting authority. That meant that shares held by Canadian shareholders would be the only ones with voting power; hence control of the company would rest in the hands of Canadians.
As I say, we have had two precedents in recent months. United Investment Life Assurance Company came before the house a few days before the summer recess. It was given third reading in July and went to the Senate. I do not know what the Senate has done, but the example of that company, I suggest, ought to be followed by the Aetna Casualty Company of Canada. I commend such a course of action to this company, through the hon. member for High Park, who follows diligently his responsibility in looking after such matters. I am sure that he will communicate with the company to tell them these thoughts-if they do not know them already-and I hope the company will come forward and say, "Yes, we voluntarily believe that what the Prime Minister says should occur, what the Minister of Trade and Commerce thinks should occur with respect to good Canadian corporate citizenship, and what the President of the Privy Council says should occur, will occur, and we shall become a Canadian owned company."

Supporting the amendment which is now before us in connection with these estimates, I should like to add an additional reason for believing that something is wrong and that the minister, the department and the government should be condemned rather than commended.
I make reference to what in my belief is the failure of the government to enforce its own regulations with respect to the terms of employment of civil servants. Information coming to my attention leads me to believe that the government is gypping its own employees-that in many cases it is not paying them for the work they are doing.
I should like to remind the minister of the actual wording of the government's own regulations with respect to the remuneration of employees:
Acting Pay
38.	(1) Subject to these Regulations, acting pay shall be paid to an employee from the date on which he is required to perform the duties of the higher position than the one held by him.
(2) Except where the Commission otherwise authorizes, acting pay shall not be paid to an employee for a period in excess of twelve continuous months.
39.	Acting pay shall not be paid to an employee who is required to perform the duties of a higher position than the one held by him for a period of less than two months.
40.	(1) Where an employee is required to perform the duties of a higher position than the one held by him, he shall be paid acting pay
(a)	if there is a scale of rates of pay for the higher position, in accordance with the provisions of section 22 as if he had been appointed to that position; and
(b)	if there is no scale of rates of pay for the higher position, at the rate of pay for that position.
That is the actual wording of the regulations with respect to acting pay in the case of federal civil servants. Mr. Chairman, I have received complaint after complaint from members of the civil service that these regulations are not being carried out. Apparently if one is in the higher echelons employed in a supervisory capacity, and if one has to do the work of someone in a higher grade there is no difficulty whatsoever about getting acting [The Chairman.]
pay, but if one happens to belong to a lower echelon-then just try and get it!
The delays go on and on forever. I was told as recently as last week by civil servants in both Montreal and in Ottawa that these people are kept waiting until either they drop their demands because they are fed up or else leave the job. These people tell me it is not only a question of gypping some of the employees-the practice is actually fraudulent; the government is defrauding its own workers by withholding their legitimate pay. I have personal knowledge of civil servants who have worked for more than a year in a higher grade without being paid the increased amounts to which they were entitled. I have in my possession statements signed by their superiors to the effect that they were doing good work and doing it in a responsible way. Yet when they asked for acting pay, they were refused.
I have seen some of the letters sent out by the deputy ministers and I maintain that these letters are full of evasion, endeavouring to circumvent the wording of the regulations and consequently cheating civil servants of their proper rate of pay. I think this is a disgraceful and disgusting situation. I can call attention to statements in my possession in which supervisors say, for example, "This man performs work over his grade in a satisfactory manner and his knowledge is presently sufficient for this type of work."
Again, I have statements such as the following: "Since this assessor works on the same types of files as a grade 3 assessor with satisfactory result, he is entitled to grade 3 pay." But the employee concerned does not get it-and he has been on this job for more than a year.
I saw a letter from the deputy minister about a week ago. I have read it and re-read it. It is nothing more or less than evasion, and I sincerely hope something will be done about this situation. Anyway, since our civil servants are receiving treatment of this kind from the minister, from the government and from the departmental heads I think there is an additional reason for voting non-confidence on this estimate.

Mr. Chairman, I shall probably disagree with my colleague and hon. friend, the mover of the subamendment, for a reason which I should like to explain as briefly as possible.
October 31, 1967

Day after day in this house, I hear honourable members ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) or the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Benson) for salary increases; others ask for the financing of the Dosco deficits, so that a few hundred or thousand people are not put out of work; I hear other members ask the government to take over a shipyard in order to keep in operation a concern which seems to have a deficit; others beg the government to prevent the Canadian National from laying off some employees because the railway wants to proceed with automation, to renovate its operations in order to do away with deficits.
I hear hon. members ask for higher pensions and generous scholarships; others complain that not enough money is allocated for research; some want protection along waterways; others anxiously await medicare; still others say that Expo has resulted in a large deficit and that centennial celebrations have cost a lot of money. All these hon. members would like to get subsidies for their ridings. Meanwhile, at another moment of the debate or at another time of day, I hear from all corners of the house members blame the government for the rising cost of living and the continuous tax increases and say that it is the fault of the government for allowing taxes to increase.
Hearing all those demands, Mr. Chairman, I conclude there is something wrong somewhere and that if we do not want the cost of living and taxes to go up, something will have to hurt somewhere in the present context.
And when I hear the official opposition chide the government for not fulfilling its duties towards the nation, I tell myself it is six of one and half a dozen of the other, because if the opposition were now in power, it would have to operate within the same financial system as the present government and it would have no more latitude.
Then, when there is talk of priorities, I feel that it is a matter of opinion, that if everyone continues to clamor for increases, as I mentioned earlier, everyone is going to pay for it; someone will have to foot the bill, because you cannot expect miracles.
We might do well to pause for a moment and to ask ourselves where such ever-increasing demands will lead us, while at the same time they cause some people to blame the government, rather illogically, with taxing away with one hand what it
Supply-Treasury Board gives with the other, which cannot be avoided anyway. Whatever party is in power, I think this is unavoidable.
We might do well to remind ourselves that our national debt now stands at about $15,971 million, and this is our net debt; our gross debt totals about $26 billion, or something like that. This represents $792.22 per capita, not per family, in Canada. Another thing about which we should remind ourselves, this national debt-and I take my province as a typical case-plus the Quebec debt, which stands at $1,524,800,000, plus the total municipal debt, average out at this time to $2,062.83 per capita in Canada.
If we add to this private debts, that is, debts to banks, finance companies and other similar institutions, it would mean a further amount of $7,062,000,000, or approximately $353.10 per capita. Therefore, the total indebtedness of every Canadian would be $2,415.93. And then, I have omitted school debts, since I do not have those figures. I have not referred to mortgages either, because I did not have time to check the figures.
This means, therefore, if it is admitted for the purpose of this discussion that an average Canadian family comprises 4 persons, the father and mother and two children, that every Canadian family would be indebted for $9,663.72, and, with the interests added, that amount could be almost twice as high, at a conservative estimate, especially for long term commitments. This would represent, therefore, something like a $14,000 debt for every Canadian family.
Mr. Chairman, I think we are faced with a case where the question should be asked: Where are we going? How will all this end? Will we be able one fine day to pass the sponge and wipe out all these debts? We, who are responsible for the public weal, are we justified in continuing to ask the government for increases, benefits and subsidies without thinking that tax increases will be required? Or, Mr. Chairman, are we not faced with a drastic situation that will remind us once again that our financial system is becoming obsolete and that we will have to revise it? Please note that I am not trying to blame either the current government or the official opposition; I say that the two parties alternating at the helm are operating in the situation where they have little elbow room.
The question is probably more relevant than it might seem at first. Might it not be
October 31, 1967

Supply-Treasury Board time to revise in depth our financial and fiscal systems? Like most of my colleagues, I read the vehement protests that came up after the Carter report suggesting a review of taxation which, in some quarters, was considered as rather socialistic. I do not say that I personally approve all the conclusions of the Carter report, but I wonder if its impact might not open the eyes of all Canadians to this situation which will shortly become a dead end, a catastrophe, if not a financial bankruptcy.
Once again, Mr Chairman, I wonder, and I have said this before, if it might not be time to call what I would refer to in a term applied in other areas, the Estates General of high finance in the country, to ask them to submit to self-reform before the demands rise, before protests become more and more vehement, in short, before the demonstrations become violent in many cases due to the problems facing the Canadian people in meeting the demands of a rising cost of living and the rising taxes. Precisely due to everyone's demands, I wonder if it is not time for the Estates General of high finance to meet, examine their own conscience and say: Together with the government, we will undertake a financial reform from which will possibly ensue a parallel tax reform in depth. Possibly, the government might have to go further and borrow some of the ideas of our friends in the New Democratic party who claim that certain high-yield enterprises should be controlled by the government to help lighten the tax load? In this, I will support them more easily than in their demands to cut the minister's salary.
When I heard that, I was tempted to suggest a double salary for the minister who so patiently listened to everything which was said to him this afternoon, but then he would have to pay too much income tax. I shall be satisfied to suggest a salary increase of $1 as a reward for his patience and his good spirits without too much of a burden in terms of income tax.
Mr. Chairman, we are all serious-minded people in this house and the situation is not going to be corrected by talking like Tories or Grits, with that kind of racing game in order to know who will be in power tomorrow, who will have succeeded in further demolishing the party in power, who will have improved the situation, who will have helped to correct it. It will not even be with those insulting criticisms against the government from some high finance leaders, when

in fact they take part in the formulation of the financial policy and share in the responsibility of the situation for which they blame the government.
I say that we are bogged down. All those of goodwill will have to get together and have a close look at the whole financial or taxation system. They will have to decide once and for all to propose basic reforms, fundamental reforms. Conservatives and N.D.P. suggestions will have to be used, and perhaps some from the Creditistes also, as they are not all wrong. Above all, anyone who is entrusted with the common good, all of us here, we shall have to forget our political or electoral ambitions for a few days and decide that we shall get at the root of the problem.
Mr. Chairman, I merely want to recall this: shall we wait till there is a popular uprising to strike at the root of the evil? Let us remember that it is no use preaching to a hungry man. And we already have alarming omens of a revolt threatening every day to generalize, to be increasingly violent.
I think it is time for everyone to sit down and to examine one's conscience, and that will not be done merely by blaming the minister for an alleged carelessness. I for one say that the present minister, who is on the carpet this afternoon, does his utmost, as did his Conservative predecessors-perhaps I was not here to judge them but I was keeping a close watch on the business of the house. I think that all members of this house are men of goodwill who try to do their best, but have to operate within a system leaving them very little latitude.
And I have no desire to blame the minister; I feel inclined instead to extend to him my sympathy and my co-operation, as I would do if a Conservative minister were in his place tonight and would probably be doing his best too, in the circumstances, and would not feel inclined to say that it is because of his inefficiency that things are going wrong.

Mr. Chairman, no doubt it will be a pleasant change for the committee to move from the vitriolic fields of the Privy Council to the gentle, bucolic glades of agriculture.
Rather than take the time of the committee at the present time with a detailed review of the specific items in the estimates I feel it might be useful to spend a few moments reviewing very briefly some aspects of the situation in Canadian agriculture. The timing is particularly appropriate in that we now have available some of the data collected by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics in the 1966 census.
To me it is of particular interest to note the adjustments that have taken place and are taking place in Canadian agriculture, adjustments which will produce in Canada a more viable and effective agriculture and which should do much to correct the difficulties that have plagued not only Canadian agriculture but agriculture pretty well all over the world in the past few years. I think the generic problem of agriculture in the past few years has been the trend to larger units, the urban trend, the movement of population from the land to urban municipalities. This results not only from new opportunities in urban centres but from the new efficiencies in agriculture which enable a far higher rate of production than was possible in the past and which render a need for fewer people in agriculture than used to be the case in the past.
It is worthy of note that during the five years from 1961 to 1966 Canadian agricultural production has risen very significantly. Returns to farmers have moved upwards and this has all been accomplished with no significant increase of land under production, although there has been a spectacular increase in recent years in the percentage of improved land making up the total land area in Canada's farms.

October 31, 1967

Cash income from the sale of farm produce in the year 1961 totalled $2.89 billion. In 1966 the figure stood at $4.23 billion, a growth of 46 per cent.
In the same time total net income, that is, realized gross earnings minus operating and depreciation charges and adjustments for the value of inventory changes, rose from $935 million to $1,978 million, a growth of 112 per cent. But perhaps the most outstanding feature of these changes has been that these increases in farm income have been brought about by growth in productivity and efficiency on the part of Canadian farmers. This is well demonstrated by the fact that in 1961 the Canadian consumer spent 23.8 per cent of his or her income on the purchase of food, while in 1966 this dropped to 21.9 per cent, one of the lowest levels of all the countries of the world.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
How was this accomplished? As I mentioned earlier, one important factor is the continued adjustment by the farmer himself. While I think it is true that from time to time there has been consumer unrest, when they have complained regarding the increasing cost of food, in fairness to the farm community it should be pointed out, as I have tried to point out today, that the Canadian wage earner is spending a smaller and smaller percentage of his income on food. This can be attributed to the efficiency and greater productivity of the farmer. Surely the Canadian consumer cannot expect to find higher and higher wages in the marketplaces where he or she labours, and at the same time not expect that the farmer should have a commensurately increasing income for his efforts.
Looking first at average farm size, in 1961 the average Canadian farm consisted of 359 acres. By 1966 this had risen by 13 per cent to 404 acres. While the figures vary greatly from area to area, with farms in Saskatchewan averaging 763 acres, all areas showed distinct growth in farm size.
In respect of livestock and poultry products, specialization has continued to be the order of the day. For example the average number of hogs on farms has risen almost 50 per cent in 5 years from 24 head to 35 head. In respect of dairy cattle a like trend is indicated. While adjustments were slower a 20 per cent increase in average herd size was experienced during the period 1961 to 1966.
The importance of this adjustment in livestock production units can best be realized

when one notes that returns from livestock make up about 55 per cent of the farm cash income that Canadian farmers received in 1966. Beef production continues to grow in importance, with the percentage of farm cash income from livestock and livestock products attributable to the beef enterprise rising in the past ten years from 28 per cent to 38 per cent.
Although as a result of climatic conditions wheat production has fluctuated, and 1967 represented a downward fluctuation, without exception the agricultural community has been astounded by the actual crops grown. This would not have been the case were it not for the changed technology, the improvements that farmers have wrought and the results of research. Normally western farmers can expect 9 to 12 inches of rainfall during the growing season. This year in Alberta and Manitoba this was down 31 per cent and 27 per cent respectively below normal. Saskatchewan received an average of only 4.55 inches which is 50 per cent below normal. This was lower than our traditionally bad year of 1937 when an average of 5.8 inches of rain fell in Saskatchewan from April to September. That year Saskatchewan farmers produced only 36 million bushels of wheat at 2.6 bushels per acre. This year the average for this big wheat province is forecast at 15.8 bushels per acre.
These adjustments and the technological changes have been assisted by government policies, in part through the operations of the Farm Credit Corporation. In view of some comment the other day in this house I should like to point out that last year Canadian farmers grew the biggest wheat crop in history. While they and they alone can claim the credit for that magnificent production, I suggest that government policy and the general burgeoning of the economy of the country have brought about some effect, and certainly contributed to the farmers' confidence in growing that size of crop.
Also last year the largest wheat crop in Canadian history was sold. Certainly in the past few years the order of the day has been not only for more and more production but greater sales of wheat. When we think of the past I think the largest sale was one of 340 million bushels. Last year we were playing an entirely new game in sales when they exceeded 500 million bushels on the export markets.
Hon. gentlemen opposite were most concerned last year about the price of wheat.

We still are.
October 31, 1967

Since this government took office the price has been higher than it has ever been, and certainly higher than it was during the administration of hon. members opposite. This year hon. members opposite were concerned about the sales of wheat. I suggest that they should whistle both tunes at the same time, or stop whistling from one side of their mouths on one occasion and from the other side on another.
Very clearly the farmers are not only concerned with price but also with volume sales. Certainly it would be of little benefit to western farmers to have a very high price if that high price pushed them out of the world markets. For those of us who have the responsibility of government and for sales on behalf of the western farmer, our aim must ever be to achieve the best possible price consonant with the maximum volume of sales. That has been this government's policy.
Hon. gentlemen opposite made some suggestions the other day in respect of the Kennedy round and the world wheat agreement. There was criticism of the officials attending the Kennedy round and an implication was made by one hon. member to the effect that a satisfactory agreement had not been arranged. There was also the suggestion that the prior world wheat agreement should have been renewed, rather than negotiating a new wheat agreement under the aegis of the Kennedy round. If the prior world wheat agreement had been renewed there would have been a 21 cent loss in minimum payments to the Canadian farmer. If that is the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite, they have changed their minds since last year when they were advocating higher prices. Since hon. gentlemen opposite sometimes express the view that they are the only ones who are in any way concerned with the welfare of the western farmer, let me point out that for all their protestations, during their tenure in office they never did see fit to guarantee payments to the western wheat farmer at the minimum new world wheat price, as this government has done.
We never had to do that.

I might also point out that the agreement has been made at $1.95J a bushel, not $1.64 a bushel which was the minimum during the tenure of office of hon. gentlemen opposite. Even at $1.64 the government of that day was not prepared to guarantee the minimum payment to the western farmer.
A comparison of data with data from previous census figures gives some concept of
Supply-Agriculture
the range and pace of the changes taking place in agriculture. The most remarkable feature is the increasing rate of adjustment toward larger farm businesses. For example the exceptional increases can be seen in the number of farms with sales over $15,000. As we can see, these have more than doubled in number in the ten years from 1951 to 1961. This number has more than doubled again in the five years from 1961 to 1966. This is not only a credit to the ingenuity and efficiency of the Canadian farmer, but in some way it must be concerned with the general prosperity and well-being of the country. Surely that had something to do with making this possible within the last five years.
The number of farms with sales between $10,000 and $15,000 has followed a similar pattern. It is also significant, although the total number of farms continues to decline, that all classes of farms with sales of $5,000 or more have increased substantially and the numbers in all classes below this level have decreased. The 1951 census showed over 85 per cent of all farms with sales of less than $5,000. Only 55.2 per cent were in these classes in 1966, the greatest decline being those farms with the lowest level of sales. In numbers of farms, 21.2 thousand had sales of $10,000 in 1951, while 95,000 farms were in this category in 1966.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
There are, of course, a great many factors involved in these changes but there is little doubt that the availability of capital on appropriate terms has greatly assisted these improvements in the structure of agriculture. Without indulging in complacency, we have good reason to believe that the operations of the Farm Credit Corporation have been a strong influence in encouraging-and more importantly-facilitating these necessary changes. Without detracting from the essential contributions of improved crop varieties and livestock, better machinery and technology or the improving managerial ability of farmers, the advantages of any of these can only be fully realized if there is capital available so they can be combined into efficiently organized farm businesses.
In this connection it is of interest to note that in the fiscal year 1961-62 the Farm Credit Corporation made a total of just under 6,000 loans in an amount of about $69 million. In 1966, doubtless due to the increased awareness of farmers as to the need for and validity of the utilization of technological advances, the loans had risen to over 12,000,

Mr. Speaker, a short while ago I asked the following question which was recorded in Hansard of September 25:
My question is directed to the Prime Minister in the absence of the Minister of Labour. Have the Minister of Labour and the officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation approved the formula of compensation devised by the city of Toronto and approved by the provincial authorities for home owners whose homes were expropriated in what is known as the Donmount urban renewal area in Toronto?
The reason for that question was that the commissioner for development in the city of Toronto had devised a complicated formula for additional compensation to owners in the Donmount urban renewal area and had received provincial consent for this formula for which he was now awaiting federal consent. What has happened in the meantime is that on the advice of a city solicitor it has been determined that under the law this formula could not be used in determining the compensation, and that the home owners are bound by the provisions of the expropriation procedures act, which is an Ontario statute.
The reason for my concern is that Donmount is one of the many urban renewal areas across the country which has had to deal with the major problem of compensation to home owners. This problem in the designated areas has arisen because of certain confusion among the city officials in determining due compensation. The owners in these urban renewal areas have found that when they received compensation for the homes they own and have then gone out to the marketplace to find another home they were paying from 15 to 25 per cent more for an equivalent home in another area of the city. Many of them have had to assume larger mortgages than existed on their former homes and have had to pay larger mortgage payments, which include the high interest rates that people have to pay for homes in Canada today.
Of course the people most seriously hurt have been old age pensioners and people on fixed incomes who had no intention of moving and were satisfied to remain in the area
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion for the rest of their lives, but have found themselves forced to move, have received low payments for their homes, and then had to pay high prices for homes in other areas, at the same time having to make payments from incomes on which they could get along quite well in their former homes.
As a result a great public clamour arose not only from the owners in the urban renewal scheme but from the public at large.
As a result, the principle of a home for a home has emerged. This has caused a great deal of concern to city officials, and it needs clarification because many people thought that the term "value to the owner" only meant the market value, and many people were led to believe by city officials and others that this was the basis of compensation for these people.
The principle has been expressly set forth in the Exchequer Court of Canada in the decision on the National Capital Commission v. Millen. There are five main principles with regard to due compensation which must be taken into account. First is the acquiring of equivalent premises, which is why the slogan "a home for a home" has achieved such prominence today: second, the payment for temporary accommodation and storage of furniture during the period involved while finding equivalent premises; third, the payment of moving expenses and fourth, the payment for the almost certain impossibility of utilizing the furnishings which had been acquired for the expropriated property. Then, fifth, and this is the important part, Mr. Speaker, compensation should be paid for personal inconvenience if people have had to acquire this new property, for miscellaneous expenses and for the general destruction of family life incidental to moving a family from one neighbourhood to another.
The question arises, Mr. Speaker, just what is the government doing to give leadership to the implementation of these principles with regard to compensation in connection with these urban renewal schemes? Thus far the onus has fallen on city officials, and there have been occasions when city officials have asked the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) what principles apply with regard to compensation for these people. The general disruption theory and the theory of a home for a home have not been clarified by the Minister of Labour. I ask the minister just what leadership he has given in connection with this problem of deciding the proper principles for compensation for homes in these renewal scheme areas, so that the schemes

The formula for compensation that will apply to the urban renewal program has been approved by the Minister of Labour. The hon. member shakes his head, but until I am notified otherwise I take it as a fact. I checked this aspect at six o'clock in anticipation of the question, and I was a little perplexed, in view of the answer, as to why the question was still on the late show. I was assured by the department that the answer was, yes.
The question of lack of leadership which the hon. member infers may be more a question of ignorance on the part of provincial and civic authorities, not only in Toronto but across Canada, in not being aware of the legislation available to them. I wonder whether, under his definition of leadership, we are obliged to take the civic authorities by the nose and acquaint them with a law of which their own legal departments should be well aware.
The original formula, which my friend has failed to point out, was unsatisfactory to the people affected. I agree that the principle of market value is not good enough. Some compensation must be paid for disruption, and a home for a home is a fair exchange. If, as a result of inflation or any other factors, the compensation paid is not sufficient to permit a person to acquire another home, then additional compensation should be paid to these people. Certain people in Toronto took such strong objection to the original compensation that they fought the battle for additional funds.
I must remind the hon. member that if the original formula was unsatisfactory it was not the fault of the federal government. We agreed to absorb 50 per cent of the compensation paid. The formula was designed by the provincial and civic authorities, and we had no jurisdiction over it. Provincial law was to


establish what the compensation should be and we agreed to go along with it. We waited until the new formula was introduced, and we readily agreed to the new formula and to the additional compensation to which the hon. member has alluded.
I apologize if he has not been notified directly that this additional compensation has been approved by the federal government. Again I assure the hon. member I am giving him the information I received as late as six o'clock. I suggest to him that this is not a question of lack of leadership, perhaps, so much as a lack of understanding of the legislation that is available to civic and provincial authorities. EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-VIET NAM-REACTION TO U.S. OFFER TO CEASE FIRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 12, 1967, as reported at page 3012 of Hansard, I asked this question:
In view of the minister's statements yesterday and today in reference to the government's position, does the minister take the position that if they do not come to the negotiating table the United States should withdraw from Vie Nam?
Then the Speaker said the question was somewhat argumentative, through an almost identical question was then asked and answered. With respect, any question asked by the opposition that has any potential political sensitivity or that seeks to find out information where a government stands in reference to any domestic or international problem can be categorized as argumentative. I feel that we have been prevented from getting information from a government which refuses informative answers. To say the least, they are evasive. Gag the opposition and no real information will be forthcoming.
To come to the subject, every Canadian, in particular all members of parliament, desires peace with all his heart, and abhors war and all the barbarism that it encompasses, and I firmly believe that so do all Americans. However, world power is in a far different position than a country which has not that status. Difference of opinion on this matter arises as to the method to be used to achieve peace and security in this world. Sir Winston Churchill once said the devastating atomic weapons themselves are the greatest deterrent against war. World war II brought war to the civilian women and children. Those
October 31. 1967	COMMONS
who have seen evidence of attack by bombing are always reminded of the words "man's inhumanity to humanity".
Does the minister believe that the United States of America should not have become embroiled or entangled in Viet Nam? Does he believe if the bombing stopped Ho Chi Minh would come to the peace conference table? Does the minister believe that if Ho Chi Minh fails to come to that conference table the United States would get out of Viet Nam? Does the minister agree with Prime Minister Wilson's position in reference to Viet Nam? Do Australia, Japan and other SEATO treaty members agree with the minister's position? If not, why not? Will Ho Chi Minh come to the peace table if the United States agrees again to the cessation of bombing?
It must not be forgotten in considering all these difficult questions-and I do not know the answers-that in January-February of 1966 the United States did cease bombing for 37 days. And did not Ho Chi Minh and the Viet Cong build up their forces in consequence and infiltrate the South Vietnamese area? Were there not five pauses by the United States in bombing over a period of two years and eight months?
But have not the United States and the U.S.S.R. some common ground in that both believe in some form of containment policy in reference to China? Surely Canada's interest must always be for permanent peace, and international affairs must transcend narrow political partisanship. In considering these questions, may I quote from a statement made by the secretary of state of the United States on October 12, 1967. This is what he said on that occasion, and I am sure these words are well known to the minister:
President Johnson has emphasized, time and time again, his interest in a prompt and peaceful settlement of the present struggles in Southeast Asia. Just two weeks ago, in San Antonio, he said:
''The United States is willing to stop all aerial and naval bombardment of North Viet Nam when this will lead promptly to productive discussions. We, of course, assume that while discussions proceed, North Viet Nam would not take advantage of the bombing cessation or limitation."
Can there be a more reasonable proposal? Is there anything unfair about such a simple proposition? Is it not clear that if Hanot is interested in peace it could say "yes" publicly or privately to the President's offer?
A rejection, or a refusal even to discuss such a formula for peace, requires that we face some sober conclusions. It would mean that Hanoi has not abandoned its effort to seize South Viet Nam by force. It would give reality and credibility to captured documents which describe a "fight and negotiate" strategy by Viet Cong and the North Vietnamese forces. It would reflect a view ip Hanoi

I know the minister will agree with me when I say that the United States, which is our neighbour, is a world leader. It is the leader of the western world, and that country is in a difficult position. But I felt that I asked a reasonable question.
The minister was complimented for taking a firm position. He left the quiet diplomacy about which the Prime Minister and he himself boasted, and took a position against the United States at a very sensitive time. I should like to know what the answers are. Where does the government stand? If Hanoi would not come to the conference table previously when the United States ceased bombing, what evidence has the minister tonight that Hanoi would come to the peace table if the United States stopped bombing now?

Mr. Speaker, in three minutes it will not be possible to answer all questions which have been asked but I should like to answer the essential question which was asked of me the other day and again tonight.
I have made it clear on a number of recent occasions that there is no absolute guarantee that a suspension of the bombing will necessarily and immediately bring about a beginning of talks leading to peace in Viet Nam.
What seems to me to be very clear, and what I am convinced of, is that talks of any kind cannot get started unless the bombing is stopped. If it is stopped I believe that an entirely new situation will then exist in which considerable pressure can be brought to bear on North Viet Nam to enter into peace talks. A situation in which the bombing is no longer being carried out would force the North Vietnamese to react, especially since they and their closest friends have placed such overwhelming emphasis on this point. If this point were met, I should think that a number of countries which have particularly close relations with North Viet Nam would use their influence constructively and in the interests of peace.

1 think it can be assumed, too, that Canada and other countries like Denmark, Norway and Sweden which have spoken out as Canada and other like minded countries have, would appeal urgently to Hanoi to seize the opportunity opened by the suspension of bombing to meet for talks. An inflexible position on the part of North Viet Nam, and an adamant refusal on their part to show a willingness to break out of the prevailing tragic and destructive impasse would, I think, place a serious responsibility on them for the war's continuation.
If however they did not respond in the way world opinion would urge them to do, I admit that the resulting situation would be serious. As I have said before, it could run the risk of reversion to exclusively military measures of perhaps a more powerful kind and, in this sense, I recognize that there is a calculated risk. If it fails-and in all realism I think it is only right to keep this possibility in mind-there will be new problems and new anxieties to deal with, but it would be impossible to forecast what precise possibilities would then be open to countries which have consistently tried to help to foster the beginning of negotiations.
As I said to the external affairs committee last week, any foreign minister and any government can shape a country's foreign policy only in the light of the actual circumstances before them at the time. In the hypothetical case under consideration this might well include some new factors; much would depend on what had happened in the period immediately following the suspension of the bombing.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity given to me tonight to pursue the question I raised a few days ago in the house about the important issue of air pollution in the Port Mait-land-Dunnville area of southwestern Ontario.
The crux of my question the other day was to find out whether the federal government through its responsible officials is investigating the reports of alleged harmful effects to man, livestock and vegetation attributed to fluoride fumes which have been emitted from a chemical fertilizer in the Port Maitland-Dunnville area.


e (10:20 p.m.)
Serious accusations, charges and counter charges have produced alarm and confusion among the people concerned. It has been reported in the press that the damaging effects of fluoride in the atmosphere over the Port Maitland and Dunnville area were known to the responsible provincial authorities as early as 1963.
It is also known that under an arbitration decision taken last year, the chemical fertilizer plant in the Port Maitland area was ordered to compensate the local farmers for livestock and plant diseases caused by fluoride fumes. Recently local farmers have made serious complaints about damage to human health.
A lung specialist from Detroit has been reported as saying that fluoride fumes are poisoning farmers, cattle and crops. I am interested in finding out tonight whether federal officials are investigating the charges and claims made by the affected parties in the Dunnville area; whether any federal assistance in this matter has been offered or requested; whether any federal monitoring centre has been established in this area and whether any air sampling from the Dunnville area has been studied by federal technicians. We want to know what specific steps have been taken.
I would like to encourage the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) to be bold, innovating, and reformist in the fight against air pollution.
